title: Labor moves to neutralise ‘widow’s tax’ and trust issues
full_text:
Labor has sought to fix its “widow’s tax” by proposing to amend budget changes that would have denied Australians who inherited a property from their spouse access to negative gearing.
Under draft legislation released late on Tuesday for a two-week consultation period, widowers, divorcees and victims of domestic violence will not face less favourable tax treatment on investment properties previously owned with a spouse or partner.
The “widow’s tax” was an unintended consequence of Labor’s budget changes to negative gearing that meant future investors would only be able to use rental losses to reduce tax on other income if the property was newly built. Although the original legislation grandfathered existing properties bought before the May 12 budget date cut-off, properties that were inherited after this date would cease to be eligible for the exemption once the changes come into force from July 2027.
Jim Chalmers’ move to open up another rushed two-week consultation period on new draft pieces of legislation for the second tranche of the government’s capital gains tax and negative gearing reforms seeks to neutralise issues over the “ widow’s tax ” and the treatment of testamentary trusts.
Yet criticisms of Labor’s tax changes persist, including the fact the government acceded to the Greens’ demand to limit superannuation funds from borrowing money to buy residential property, for which Treasury acknowledged in new documents they had produced no regulatory impact statement.
It came as fresh analysis showed that Labor’s proposed tax and superannuation policies were disproportionately hurting women.
Data from the Super Members Council show that Labor’s refusal to force business to pay superannuation for those under the age of 18 working less than 30 hours a week will leave 528,000 teenage workers across Australia missing out on $411m in super this financial year.
This new figure is up 25,000 people on two years ago.
“Young women are more likely to be affected by the exclusion because they are more likely to work part-time than teenage men, with SMC analysis showing a typical young woman misses out on around $2500 in super contributions before turning 18, about 6 per cent more than a typical young man,” SMC executive general manager, advocacy, James Gunn said.
“By retirement age, this loss grows to around $11,200 for women, compared with $10,600 for men.”
The council estimated that a typical teenager who spends at least two years in part-time work before turning 18 could miss out on around $2500 in super contributions by age 18. That lost super could compound to an $11,000 reduction by retirement in today’s dollars.
Labor resolved at its national conference last month that the party supported superannuation for “all workers”, including under 18s, but it voted against an amendment to its super bill that would have forced businesses to pay super to those under 18 who worked fewer than 30 hours a week.
Australian Greens spokeswoman for finance, employment and workplace relations Barbara Pocock said Labor was lying to the public. “They say they support teen super but they vote against it in parliament.”
“Labor is leaving under 18s underpaid and undercutting their futures. A party that leaves young workers out isn’t the party for workers,” Senator Pocock said.
“Young people deserve every dollar they’ve earned, and that includes their super. “
Senator Pocock said the Greens would introduce a private senator’s bill in the next parliament sitting fortnight. “Labor will have a choice: they can support super for all young workers or vote against it yet again.”
On Tuesday, a Freedom of Information request to the Treasury Department lodged by opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg revealed that there were “no documents” that related to a regulatory impact statement on the government’s widow’s tax, introduced at the May budget.
The Coalition accused Labor of having “failed to do proper analysis” about the impact of its move to stop self-managed super funds from borrowing money to buy residential property.
The government agreed to clamp down on SMSF limited recourse borrowing arrangements in a deal with the Greens to pass tax changes through the Senate.
A consequence of the change is that it would especially affect middle-aged and elderly women, given divorced women with few assets often set up an SMSF to use it as a guarantee to buy a house.
“They did no regulatory analysis,” Senator Bragg said. “They hate individual investors.
“And so they’ve gone out of their way to ban individual investors from doing things that big super funds like Cbus and Hesta can do. They did it at the behest of the super-industrial complex.
“And what they’ve ended up doing is creating a definition which is at odds with their main tax hike because they’ve neglected to make a distinction between new and existing housing.”
Contacted for comment, the Treasurer’s office said “multiple inquiries” had flagged concerns with SMSF limited recourse borrowing arrangements, including a 2014 inquiry under a Coalition government. “These arrangements constitute less than 1 per cent of total residential property borrowing and less than 0.5 per cent of new residential borrowing each year,” a spokesman said.
“This is a housing spokesman whose policy is to cut housing.”
On the exposure drafts published by his department, Dr Chalmers said in a media release that they reflected “the government’s commitment to consult on more complex elements of tax reforms announced in the budget”.
“Consistent with other significant tax reforms, the government will continue to finalise implementation of the reforms in further tranches of legislation.”
